# QM Intermediate: Course overview {#intermediate-course}

QM Intermediate builds on the probability, inference, and R skills from QM
Basic. The central question changes from "What does this sample show?" to
"How is an outcome related to several variables at the same time?"

For a founder these are the questions behind most decisions. What does an
extra euro of advertising bring? Does a lower price sell more, once the
season is taken into account? Does the new page beat the old one? Regression
is the tool that R and every AI assistant use to answer them. This course
teaches you to read its output, to check it, and to decide with it.

::: {.outcomes}
<span class="label">By the end of QM Intermediate, you can</span>

- formulate simple and multiple-regression questions from E&BI problems
- fit, diagnose, and interpret linear regression models in R
- distinguish a coefficient, fitted value, residual, and uncertainty
  interval
- interpret tests against zero, $R^2$, and F-tests for model usefulness
- use dummy predictors, interactions, and polynomial terms
- explain how controls change an estimate without automatically making it
  causal
- read the central regression evidence in a business or management paper.
:::

## The data we use

All lectures use the Shark Tank teaching file. One row is one pitch on the
US television show *Shark Tank*: 1,441 pitches from Seasons 1 to 16.
Founders ask a panel of investors, the sharks, for money in exchange for a
share of their company. The file records what they asked for, the share they
offered, and whether a deal was agreed on air and on which terms.

- The variables are listed in
  [Basic Lecture 1, "The variables in the Shark Tank file"](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd#b01-variable-table).
- The [welcome page](../index.qmd) describes where the data come from and
  what they cannot show: these are selected television pitches, not a random
  sample of all ventures.
- Lectures 1 to 3 study valuations, in millions of dollars: the valuation a
  founder claims and the valuation agreed on air. From Lecture 4 on, the
  outcome is the equity offered, in percent, and the requested amount is
  measured in thousands of dollars. These units keep axes and coefficients
  easy to read.

No other dataset is needed for the lectures. The mock exam uses a second,
invented dataset that you download from its page.

## What this course builds on

QM Intermediate uses a small set of ideas from QM Basic. Each row of the
table says where this book explains the idea, so you can look it up when a
lecture uses it.

| Idea | Used here for | Where to read it again |
|---|---|---|
| Mean, variance, standard deviation | slopes, residual spread | [Basic Lecture 3](../basic/b03-discrete-distributions.qmd) |
| Covariance, correlation, conditional mean | the slope formula, what a regression line estimates | [Basic Lecture 5](../basic/b05-joint-covariance-correlation.qmd) |
| Sample and population, estimator and estimate | $\hat\beta_1$ as an estimate of $\beta_1$ | [Basic Lecture 7](../basic/b07-samples-estimators.qmd) |
| Standard error | the "Std. Error" column of R output | [Basic Lecture 8](../basic/b08-sampling-distributions.qmd) |
| Confidence interval, t distribution | intervals for coefficients | [Basic Lecture 9](../basic/b09-t-confidence-intervals.qmd) |
| p-value, test against zero | the "t value" and "Pr(>\|t\|)" columns | [Basic Lecture 10](../basic/b10-testing-errors-power.qmd) |

The preparation for Lecture 1 has a ten-minute warm-up on five quantities
from the last four rows: estimate, standard error, t value, p-value, and
confidence interval.

### If you took QM Basic before 2026

The Basic chapters in this book are new. If you took the course in its
earlier form, you know the ideas in the table, but three things look
different here.

- **Values come from R, not from tables.** Where you looked up a z or t
  table, this book uses `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, and `qt()`. In the exam the
  values you need are in the R output.
- **Notation for multipliers.** You may know $z_{\alpha/2}$ and
  $t_{\alpha/2;\,n-1}$. This book writes $z_{0.975}=1.96$ and
  $t_{0.975,\,df}$, the way R does: `qnorm(0.975)` and `qt(0.975, df)`. The
  numbers are the same.
- **Tests are tests against zero.** A test of "the mean equals 15" is
  written as "the difference from 15 equals zero". Regression output tests
  every coefficient against zero in the same way. All tests in this course
  are two-sided.

It is worth one hour to read the lecture material of
[Basic Lecture 9](../basic/b09-t-confidence-intervals.qmd) and
[Basic Lecture 10](../basic/b10-testing-errors-power.qmd) before the course
starts. The [welcome page](../index.qmd) explains how every chapter of this
book is built, and [How to succeed in this course](../resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
shows what a week looks like.

## Course sequence

| Chapter | Central question |
|---|---|
| Lecture 1 | What line best summarises the relationship between two variables? |
| Lecture 2 | What does the model assume, and what do its residuals reveal? |
| Lecture 3 | How precise are the coefficients, and is the model useful at all? |
| Tutorial 1 | Can you fit, diagnose, and communicate a simple regression? |
| Lecture 4 | How do we interpret one predictor while holding others fixed? |
| Lecture 5 | How do categories enter a model, and are terms jointly useful? |
| Lecture 6 | When does a slope depend on another variable or change across $x$? |
| Tutorial 2 | Can you build and defend a multiple-regression specification? |
| Code sheet | Which R commands and formulas are required for the assessment? |
| Mock exam | Can you integrate the complete course in a 100-point assessment? |

External video explanations come from Stanford's
[Statistical Learning series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLoROMvodv4rOzrYsAxzQyHb8n_RWNuS1e).
The supporting print text is James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani,
*An Introduction to Statistical Learning*, 2nd edition, especially Chapter 3.
For a more formal treatment, consult
[Nieuwenhuis, *Statistical Methods for Business and Economics*](https://tilburguniversity.on.worldcat.org/oclc/317545871),
especially Chapters 19--22. Each lecture chapter contains the definitions,
notation, examples, and practice required for this course.

## The weekly rhythm

One lecture per week, with tutorials the day after the lecture in weeks 45
and 48. The [How to succeed in this course](../resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
page lays out the week with printable checklists.

Bring a charged laptop to every lecture, with RStudio and your course
project open. All code shown in the lecture is in the chapter, ready to copy.
You can run each step yourself while it is explained and get the same
numbers and figures on your own screen.

## Tutorials and assessment

Two tutorials, one after Lecture 3 and one after Lecture 6, combine
interpretation with hands-on R work. If an R workflow has become rusty,
return to the [R Refresher](../resources/r-refresher.qmd) or the earlier
[Programming for E&BI](https://walshc.github.io/ebi-prog/) textbook.

The exam is taken in TestVision, with R available. You work with data in R
and write your answers in TestVision. The
[QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) is provided at the exam. Use it
during the tutorials too, so that you know where everything is.

The [QM Intermediate Mock Exam](mock-exam.qmd) is open from the first week.
Look at it early to see what the exam asks. After Tutorial 2, attempt it in
R under timed conditions. A practice exam in TestVision itself appears in
your TestVision account once it is published. You log in with your
university account, and there is no separate link. The university explains
TestVision for students
[on this page](https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/students/studying/exams/e-assessment/testvision).
